title: The prostration of thanks
hook: a single prostration at good news (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sujud al-sahw, the prostrations that mend a slip, and your line: mistakes are expected. What did you mend in one small step? Today, a prostration for the opposite of a mistake. Day one thousand eighty-nine.

Ka'b ibn Malik has been waiting a long time. He stayed home from a military expedition with no excuse, and when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ returned, Ka'b told the plain truth instead of inventing one. Since then, by his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari, people have stopped speaking to him. Then one morning, after the dawn prayer, sitting on the roof of his house, he hears a voice shouting from a hill: Ka'b ibn Malik, good news! Before he stands, before he runs to anyone, before he says a word, his body answers. He falls down in prostration. Today's word is that fall.
screen: `HE TOLD THE PLAIN TRUTH.` → `A VOICE FROM THE HILL.` → `HE FALLS DOWN IN PROSTRATION.`

segments.voice: Sujud al-shukr means the prostration of thanks: a single prostration, on its own, outside the regular prayer, made when good news arrives or a harm is lifted. First, the Prophet's own habit. Abu Dawud records that when something came to him that delighted him, or he was given good news, he would fall down in prostration, giving thanks to God. No bowing first, no units, no closing salam. Just down. Second, why the body and not only the mouth. In the five prayers the prostration is the lowest point, the forehead on the floor. Using that same posture for joy says something. The place of greatest humility is also the place of thanks. Third, the promise behind it. Pickthall's translation of surah fourteen has God say: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Thanks, in that verse, is not just good manners. It opens a door. Fourth, the details, where scholars differ. Some hold that because it is a prostration, it needs wudu and facing the qibla, like prayer. Others say it isn't a prayer at all, so good news can be answered on the spot, as it comes. Within the Maliki school a well-known view did not encourage it, while others in the same school accepted it. Go back to Ka'b on his roof. He didn't check whether he had wudu or which way he faced. The report just says he fell down. Whatever a person's school decides about the details, the first move in the story is the same. Good news comes, and the forehead goes to the ground.
screen: `DOWN AT GOOD NEWS.` · `THE LOWEST PLACE, FOR JOY.` · `IF YE GIVE THANKS.` · `WUDU, OR ON THE SPOT?` · then, large: `IF YE GIVE THANKS, I WILL GIVE YOU MORE.`

segments.voice: The practice is to prostrate at good news. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring back one piece of good news from the last while: a test result, a message, a child's laugh, a debt paid off, a pain that eased. Let it come back in full. If you pray, you can make a single prostration of thanks now, or keep the habit ready for the next good news. If you don't, you can bow your head, or rest your palms flat on the floor, and let the body say thanks before the mouth does. The bell holds the time.
Sujud al-shukr. The prostration of thanks: one prostration, on its own, when good news comes. Today's word.
Your line: down, in thanks. Today, when something good arrives, however small, let your body answer first: a bow of the head, a hand on the floor, a prostration. Day one thousand eighty-nine.

howItsDone: On hearing good news or being spared a harm, Muslims who keep this practice make a single prostration of thanks, outside the regular prayer; schools differ on whether wudu and facing the qibla are needed for it.

original.note: Arabic: the prostration of thanks. shukr is gratitude.

trapdoor: what you thought: prostration only happens inside the five prayers.
what it means: a single prostration, on its own, made when good news comes.
what a scholar hears: Ka'b ibn Malik falling down on his roof before checking anything, and a real debate over whether the prostration needs wudu and the qibla.

sources.quoted: If ye give thanks, I will give you more

notes: Abu Dawud 2774 (Abu Bakrah: on good news he fell down in prostration in thanks) paraphrased; confirm number.

Bukhari 4418 (Ka'b ibn Malik's long hadith: boycott after Tabuk, the voice from Mount Sal' after fajr on his roof, 'I fell down in prostration'). The count of nights is deliberately left out ('a long time'); confirm the summary.
Pickthall 14:7 quoted from memory ('And when your Lord proclaimed: If ye give thanks, I will give you more...'); confirm.

Fiqh summary: majority of Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars require the conditions of prayer; others (e.g. Ibn Taymiyyah) do not; a well-known view attributed to Malik regarded it as disliked, while others in the school accepted it. Confirm the Maliki phrasing.
